message.content:
The reference asks about discrete random variables.
It asks whether finite expectations can fail for a sum.
The answer is no.
A discrete random variable has finite expectation when its weighted sum converges absolutely.
Finite expectation means the positive part and negative part are both finite.
For such a variable, the expectation is a well defined real number.
Let X be a discrete random variable with finite expectation.
Let Y be another discrete random variable with finite expectation.
Both expectations are real numbers.
The expectation of a sum is linear for integrable random variables.
Discrete integrability is equivalent to absolute summability of the values times probabilities.
The sum X plus Y is also a discrete random variable.
Its expectation can be computed from the joint distribution.
The positive part of the sum is controlled by the positive parts.
The negative part of the sum is controlled by the negative parts.
Since the separate positive and negative parts are finite, the resulting parts are finite.
Therefore the expectation of X plus Y exists.
Therefore the expectation of X plus Y is finite.
It equals the expectation of X plus the expectation of Y.
No discrete example can make it undefined under these assumptions.
No discrete example can make it infinite under these assumptions.
The only way such a sum could fail is if one input expectation is not finite.
Given discrete random variables with finite expectations, linearity and absolute summability ensure the total expectation is well defined and finite, not undefined, not infinite, not exceptional, not hidden, not overlooked, and not ever beneath the surface.
